ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: Modeling language and cognition with deep unsupervised learning: a tutorial overview
papers.research_question: How can deep unsupervised learning be used to model language and cognitive processing, and how do structured and abstract representations emerge from deep generative learning?
papers.core_contribution: This tutorial overview argues that deep generative models offer a more plausible model of cortical learning and provide a way to bridge the gap between emergentist connectionist models and structured Bayesian models of cognition.
papers.conclusion: The focus on deep architectures and generative learning represents a crucial step forward for connectionist modeling, offering a more plausible model of cortical learning and a way to bridge the gap between emergentist connectionist models and structured Bayesian models of cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Deep unsupervised learning in hierarchical generative models can discover structured and abstract representations of sensory data.
Linear read-out accuracy of internal representations improves with the depth of the network, indicating more explicit encoding of relevant features.
The approach can simulate human-like behavior in tasks such as numerosity comparison, producing psychometric functions that match human data.
future_direction: Incorporating convolutional layers to achieve translation invariance.
Learning temporal dynamics of data to anticipate events, as in predictive coding.
Unifying connectionist and Bayesian models of cognition within a deep generative network framework.
papers.abstract: Deep unsupervised learning in stochastic recurrent neural networks with many layers of hidden units is a recent breakthrough in neural computation research. These networks build a hierarchy of progressively more complex distributed representations of the sensory data by fitting a hierarchical generative model. In this article we discuss the theoretical foundations of this approach and we review key issues related to training, testing and analysis of deep networks for modeling language and cognitive processing. The classic letter and word perception problem of McClelland and Rumelhart (1981) is used as a tutorial example to illustrate how structured and abstract representations may emerge from deep generative learning. We argue that the focus on deep architectures and generative (rather than discriminative) learning represents a crucial step forward for the connectionist modeling enterprise, because it offers a more plausible model of cortical learning as well as a way to bridge the gap between emergentist connectionist models and structured Bayesian models of cognition.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 2.1, Grade-School Math and the Hidden Reasoning Process
papers.research_question: How do language models solve grade-school math problems? Do they memorize templates or learn reasoning skills? What is the hidden reasoning process and what causes mistakes?
papers.core_contribution: Language models trained on synthetic grade-school math problems can learn reasoning skills, generalize to longer reasoning lengths, and internally compute unnecessary dependencies, indicating learning beyond the training objective.
papers.conclusion: Language models can learn genuine reasoning skills from synthetic data, and depth is more important than width for reasoning ability.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve high accuracy and generalize to longer reasoning lengths than seen during training.
Models generate shortest solutions, avoiding unnecessary computations, suggesting planning.
Probing reveals the model preprocesses necessary parameters before generation.
Models learn to compute all-pair dependencies, a skill not required by the training data.
Mistakes can be explained by probing internal states and are sometimes predictable.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not directly apply to foundation models like GPT-4 or more challenging mathematical reasoning tasks.
Uses synthetic data with modulo arithmetic, which may not reflect real-world math problems.
future_direction: Physics of Language Models: Part 2.2, How to Learn From Mistakes on Grade-School Math Problems
papers.abstract: Recent advances in language models have demonstrated their capability to solve mathematical reasoning problems, achieving near-perfect accuracy on grade-school level math benchmarks like GSM8K. In this paper, we formally study how language models solve these problems. We design a series of controlled experiments to address several fundamental questions: (1) Can language models truly develop reasoning skills, or do they simply memorize templates? (2) What is the model's hidden (mental) reasoning process? (3) Do models solve math questions using skills similar to or different from humans? (4) Do models trained on GSM8K-like datasets develop reasoning skills beyond those necessary for solving GSM8K problems? (5) What mental process causes models to make reasoning mistakes? (6) How large or deep must a model be to effectively solve GSM8K-level math questions? Our study uncovers many hidden mechanisms by which language models solve mathematical questions, providing insights that extend beyond current understandings of LLMs.

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: Interpreting and Improving Large Language Models in Arithmetic Calculation
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform arithmetic calculations, and can we improve their mathematical ability by fine-tuning specific components?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that only a small fraction of attention heads and subsequent MLPs are responsible for arithmetic calculation in LLMs, and that selectively fine-tuning these components (Precise SFT) improves mathematical performance without degrading general abilities.
papers.conclusion: The study identifies sparse attention heads and MLPs for arithmetic calculation in LLMs and shows that precise tuning of these components improves mathematical capability with less impact on non-mathematical tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Only a small fraction (<5%) of attention heads are crucial for arithmetic calculation.
These heads attend to operands and operators.
Subsequent MLPs process the information to derive the answer.
The key components are transferable across datasets and tasks.
Precise fine-tuning of these components improves mathematical performance without harming general abilities.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily focus on LLaMA2 series, generalization to other LLMs needs further investigation.
The work focuses on arithmetic calculation, and more complex mathematical problems require further research.
future_direction: Generalize to a broader range of LLMs
Investigate more complex mathematical problems
Investigate shared and distinct mechanisms across mathematical tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential across numerous applications and have shown an emergent ability to tackle complex reasoning tasks, such as mathematical computations. However, even for the simplest arithmetic calculations, the intrinsic mechanisms behind LLMs remain mysterious, making it challenging to ensure reliability. In this work, we delve into uncovering a specific mechanism by which LLMs execute calculations. Through comprehensive experiments, we find that LLMs frequently involve a small fraction (< 5%) of attention heads, which play a pivotal role in focusing on operands and operators during calculation processes. Subsequently, the information from these operands is processed through multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), progressively leading to the final solution. These pivotal heads/MLPs, though identified on a specific dataset, exhibit transferability across different datasets and even distinct tasks. This insight prompted us to investigate the potential benefits of selectively fine-tuning these essential heads/MLPs to boost the LLMs' computational performance. We empirically find that such precise tuning can yield notable enhancements on mathematical prowess, without compromising the performance on non-mathematical tasks. Our work serves as a preliminary exploration into the arithmetic calculation abilities inherent in LLMs, laying a solid foundation to reveal more intricate mathematical tasks.

papers.title: How Do Language Models Acquire Character-Level Information?
papers.research_question: How do language models acquire character-level information, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and quantifies factors contributing to character-level information acquisition in language models, categorizing them into factors arising from tokenization (merge rules and orthographic constraints) and factors independent of tokenization (semantic associations of substrings and syntactic information).
papers.conclusion: Language models do not treat words as opaque tokens but indirectly learn character-level patterns from multiple cues, including tokenization-related and linguistic factors.
papers.key_findings:
Language models acquire character-level information even when trained on manipulated corpora where form-meaning associations are removed.
Shorter subwords yield higher accuracy in the character inclusion probing task.
Merge rules in subword tokenization algorithms (like BPE) contribute to character-level information acquisition by creating statistical patterns in token sequences.
Orthographic constraints within words (e.g., spelling patterns like 'ck', 'dge') provide cues that help models infer character content.
Semantic associations of substrings (e.g., sound symbolism) and syntactic information from affixes (e.g., '-s', '-ed') are key factors independent of tokenization that aid character-level learning.
papers.limitation:
The pretraining data may contain lexical information (e.g., word lists, spelling rules) that was not fully controlled for, potentially contributing to character-level acquisition.
The nanoGPT model used is relatively small, and it remains unclear what cues contribute to character-level acquisition in larger models.
The analysis did not sufficiently examine the effects of token frequency and rare characters, which prior work suggests influence classification performance.
Experiments were conducted exclusively on English text, so generalization to other languages with different orthographic systems is an open question.
Only the FineWeb corpus was used for pretraining, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to other corpora with different characteristics.
future_direction: A more detailed analysis of the contribution of each factor identified in this study.
Applying these insights to develop model architectures and pre-training methods that can more robustly process character-level information.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) have been reported to implicitly encode character-level information, despite not being explicitly provided during training. However, the mechanisms underlying this phenomenon remain largely unexplored. To reveal the mechanisms, we analyze how models acquire character-level knowledge by comparing LMs trained under controlled settings, such as specifying the pre-training dataset or tokenizer, with those trained under standard settings. We categorize the contributing factors into those independent of tokenization. Our analysis reveals that merge rules and orthographic constraints constitute primary factors arising from tokenization, whereas semantic associations of substrings and syntactic information function as key factors independent of tokenization.

papers.title: Monotonic Representation of Numeric Properties in Language Models
papers.research_question: How are numeric properties (e.g., birth year, population) encoded in the internal representations of language models, and do these representations reflect the natural monotonic structure of such properties?
papers.core_contribution: Language models learn to represent numeric properties in low-dimensional, monotonic subspaces of their activation space, and these representations can be edited via activation patching to causally alter model output.
papers.conclusion: Language models learn monotonic representations of numeric properties, and such representations consistently emerge across different models, suggesting that pretraining captures the natural structure of numeric attributes.
papers.key_findings:
Low-dimensional subspaces (2-6 dimensions) of activation space are highly predictive (R^2 up to 0.91) of the numeric quantities a model expresses when queried.
Projections onto these subspaces reveal monotonic structure, where the position along a direction correlates with the value of the numeric attribute.
Activation patching along the found directions causally changes the model's output in a monotonic fashion, with the change in output correlating with the strength and sign of the intervention.
Monotonic representations of numeric properties exist across multiple language models (Llama 2, Falcon, Mistral) and multiple numeric properties (birth year, death year, population, elevation, latitude, longitude).
Editing along a direction for one property has side effects on other properties, suggesting some directions encode generic numeric ranges rather than being property-specific.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to popular entities, frequent numeric properties, and English queries.
Causal interventions via one-dimensional activation patching may be too simplistic, as properties are encoded in low- but not necessarily one-dimensional subspaces.
The ease of extracting information from representations is not fully quantified, and the intrinsic dimensionality of the models is unknown.
future_direction: What exactly do the found subspaces encode? Can we find more specific directions by adding constraints to minimize side effects?
Are changes along directions absolute or relative to typical value ranges?
Is the quality of numeric attribute representations connected to LM performance on tasks involving those attributes?
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) can express factual knowledge involving numeric properties such as Karl Popper was born in 1902. However, how this information is encoded in the model's internal representations is not understood well. Here, we introduce a simple method for finding and editing representations of numeric properties such as an entity's birth year. Empirically, we find low-dimensional subspaces that encode numeric properties monotonically, in an interpretable and editable fashion. When editing representations along directions in these subspaces, LM output changes accordingly. For example, by patching activations along a "birthyear" direction we can make the LM express an increasingly late birthyear: Karl Popper was born in 1929, Karl Popper was born in 1957, Karl Popper was born in 1968. Property-encoding directions exist across several numeric properties in all models under consideration, suggesting the possibility that monotonic representation of numeric properties consistently emerges during LM pretraining. Code: https://github.com/bheinzerling/numeric-property-repr

papers.title: Bigram Subnetworks: Mapping to Next Tokens in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer language models make bigram predictions, and can we identify minimal subnetworks that are both necessary and sufficient for these predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Bigram subnetworks—minimal subsets of parameters concentrated in the first MLP layer—are both necessary and sufficient for basic next token predictions in Transformer language models and drive the transformation from current to next token activations.
papers.conclusion: Bigram subnetworks are minimal, interpretable, and critical for language model performance, and they can serve as a foundation for building up more complex circuits in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Bigram subnetworks exist in models up to 1B parameters, consist of ~10M parameters regardless of model size, and achieve bigram surprisal correlations >0.95.
Bigram subnetworks are concentrated in the first Transformer MLP layer throughout pretraining.
Bigram subnetworks recreate the first-layer transformation that aligns activations with next token predictions rather than current token representations.
Ablating bigram subnetworks drastically hurts language modeling performance, demonstrating their necessity.
Bigram subnetworks overlap significantly with subnetworks trained for optimal pruning.
papers.limitation: The paper does not definitively show that language models make intermediate bigram predictions; the tuned lens used to probe intermediate predictions may be too strong and yield false positives.
future_direction: Using bigram subnetworks as a foundation to build up and study more complex circuits.
Determining where intermediate next token predictions are encoded in language model activations.
papers.abstract: In Transformer language models, activation vectors transform from current token embeddings to next token predictions as they pass through the model. To isolate a minimal form of this transformation, we identify language model subnetworks that make bigram predictions, naive next token predictions based only on the current token. We find that bigram subnetworks can be found in fully trained language models up to 1B parameters, and these subnetworks are critical for model performance even when they consist of less than 0.2% of model parameters. Bigram subnetworks are concentrated in the first Transformer MLP layer, and they overlap significantly with subnetworks trained to optimally prune a given model. Mechanistically, the bigram subnetworks often recreate a pattern from the full models where the first layer induces a sharp change that aligns activations with next token predictions rather than current token representations. Our results demonstrate that bigram subnetworks comprise a minimal subset of parameters that are both necessary and sufficient for basic next token predictions in language models, and they help drive the transformation from current to next token activations in the residual stream. These subnetworks can lay a foundation for studying more complex language model circuits by building up from a minimal circuit.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: Memory Retrieval and Consolidation in Large Language Models through Function Tokens
papers.research_question: How is memory retrieved during inference and consolidated during pre-training in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Function Token Hypothesis to explain memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs, where function tokens activate predictive features during inference and drive feature learning during pre-training.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes and provides evidence for the Function Token Hypothesis, which explains how function tokens drive memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
During inference, a small set of function tokens activate the majority of the model's features.
Function tokens dynamically reactivate the most predictive features from the context to guide next-token prediction.
During pre-training, the prediction of content tokens following function tokens dominates the loss and drives feature expansion.
Pre-training initially focuses on learning to predict function tokens before learning content tokens.
Scaling model size primarily enhances the prediction of content tokens.
papers.limitation: The paper does not explain how function tokens acquire the ability to dynamically activate predictive features.
future_direction: How function tokens acquire the ability to dynamically activate predictive features.
How post-training modifies activation patterns in function tokens.
The dynamics of feature formation and the underlying reason for the scale-free property of token-feature activation.
papers.abstract: The remarkable success of large language models (LLMs) stems from their ability to consolidate vast amounts of knowledge into the memory during pre-training and to retrieve it from the memory during inference, enabling advanced capabilities such as knowledge memorization, instruction-following and reasoning. However, the mechanisms of memory retrieval and consolidation in LLMs remain poorly understood. In this paper, we propose the function token hypothesis to explain the workings of LLMs: During inference, function tokens activate the most predictive features from context and govern next token prediction (memory retrieval). During pre-training, predicting the next tokens (usually content tokens) that follow function tokens increases the number of learned features of LLMs and updates the model parameters (memory consolidation). Function tokens here roughly correspond to function words in linguistics, including punctuation marks, articles, prepositions, and conjunctions, in contrast to content tokens. We provide extensive experimental evidence supporting this hypothesis. Using bipartite graph analysis, we show that a small number of function tokens activate the majority of features. Case studies further reveal how function tokens activate the most predictive features from context to direct next token prediction. We also find that during pre-training, the training loss is dominated by predicting the next content tokens following function tokens, which forces the function tokens to select the most predictive features from context.

papers.title: Emergent Symbol-like Number Variables in Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What types of numeric representations emerge in neural systems, and how can we interpret neural network solutions through the lens of interpretable Symbolic Algorithms?
papers.core_contribution: We extend the Distributed Alignment Search framework with alignment functions to interpret neural network activity in terms of symbolic variables, and show that recurrent networks develop graded symbol-like number variables while transformers use anti-Markovian solutions.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the utility of causal interpretability tools and alignment functions for understanding neural representations, showing that RNNs develop graded symbol-like number variables while transformers use anti-Markovian solutions.
papers.key_findings:
Recurrent models (GRUs/LSTMs) develop graded symbol-like number variables within their neural activity.
Seemingly insignificant task variations can drastically affect alignment to Symbolic Algorithms, motivating extended DAS with alignment functions (LAFs).
Linear Alignment Functions (LAFs) can control NN behavior through neural activity aligned to interpretable Symbolic Algorithms.
Shallow Transformers use anti-Markovian solutions to numeric tasks, and theoretically, Transformers must use anti-Markovian solutions without sufficient attention layers.
Causal interventions on neural subspaces are useful for NN interpretability.
papers.abstract: What types of numeric representations emerge in neural systems, and what would a satisfying answer to this question look like? In this work, we interpret Neural Network (NN) solutions to sequence based number tasks using a variety of methods to understand how well we can interpret them through the lens of interpretable Symbolic Algorithms (SAs) -- precise programs describable by rules and typed, mutable variables. We use autoregressive GRUs, LSTMs, and Transformers trained on tasks where the correct tokens depend on numeric information only latent in the task structure. We show through multiple causal and theoretical methods that we can interpret raw NN activity through the lens of simplified SAs when we frame the activity in terms of neural subspaces rather than individual neurons. Using Distributed Alignment Search (DAS), we find that, depending on network architecture, dimensionality, and task specifications, alignments with SA's can be very high, or they can be only approximate, or fail altogether. We extend our analytic toolkit to address the failure cases by expanding the DAS framework to a broader class of alignment functions that more flexibly capture NN activity in terms of interpretable variables from SAs, and we provide theoretic and empirical explorations of Linear Alignment Functions (LAFs) in contrast to the preexisting Orthogonal Alignment Functions (OAFs). Through analyses of specific cases we confirm the usefulness of causal interventions on neural subspaces for NN interpretability, and we show that recurrent models can develop graded, symbol-like number variables in their neural activity. We further show that shallow Transformers learn very different solutions than recurrent networks, and we prove that such models must use anti-Markovian solutions -- solutions that do not rely on cumulative, Markovian hidden states -- in the absence of sufficient attention layers.

papers.title: BERT is Not an Interlingua and the Bias of Tokenization
papers.research_question: Does multilingual BERT use a common interlingual space for different languages, or does it partition representations based on linguistic relationships?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual BERT partitions representations by language rather than using a shared interlingual space, and subword tokenization biases the model towards linguistic phylogenetic structure.
papers.conclusion: Using CCA on the internal representations of BERT, we find that it is not embedding different languages into a shared space. Rather, at deeper layers, BERT partitions the space to better reflect the linguistic and evolutionary relationships between languages. We also find that subword tokenization provides a strong bias to discover linguistic and evolutionary relationships between languages.
papers.key_findings:
Representations for different languages become less similar in deeper layers of BERT.
Fine-tuning causes representations to diverge further in deeper layers.
Deeper layers undergo more change during fine-tuning compared to earlier layers.
CCA similarity between languages reveals a tree structure that mirrors linguistic phylogenetic trees.
Subword tokenization biases the model towards linguistic relationships more than word or character tokenization.
papers.abstract: Multilingual transfer learning can benefit both high-and low-resource languages, but the source of these improvements is not well understood. Cananical Correlation Analysis (CCA) of the internal representations of a pretrained, multilingual BERT model reveals that the model partitions representations for each language rather than using a common, shared, interlingual space. This effect is magnified at deeper layers, suggesting that the model does not progressively abstract semantic content while disregarding languages. Hierarchical clustering based on the CCA similarity scores between languages reveals a tree structure that mirrors the phylogenetic trees hand-designed by linguists. The subword tokenization employed by BERT provides a stronger bias towards such structure than character-and wordlevel tokenizations. We release a subset of the XNLI dataset translated into an additional 14 languages at https://www.github. com/salesforce/xnli_extension to assist further research into multilingual representations.

papers.title: An Analysis of Encoder Representations in Transformer-Based Machine Translation
papers.research_question: What kind of linguistic information (syntactic and semantic) is learned by the encoder of Transformer-based machine translation models, and how does it vary across layers and models with different translation quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes encoder representations in Transformer-based machine translation and finds that specific attention heads capture syntactic dependencies, with lower layers encoding more syntax and higher layers more semantics.
papers.conclusion: The experimental evaluation sheds light on interesting findings about dependency relations and syntactic and semantic behavior across layers in Transformer encoder representations.
papers.key_findings:
Each layer has at least one attention head that encodes a significant amount of syntactic dependencies.
Lower layers tend to encode more syntactic information, while upper layers move towards semantic tasks.
The information about the length of the input sentence starts to vanish after the third layer.
Attention can be used to transfer knowledge between high- and low-resource languages, improving translation quality.
future_direction: Extend the analysis with probing tasks to evaluate other linguistic properties.
Use a recent evaluation dataset for analysis.
Analyze the attention weights between the encoder and the decoder.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism is a successful technique in modern NLP, especially in tasks like machine translation. The recently proposed network architecture of the Transformer is based entirely on attention mechanisms and achieves new state of the art results in neural machine translation, outperforming other sequence-to-sequence models. However, so far not much is known about the internal properties of the model and the representations it learns to achieve that performance. To study this question, we investigate the information that is learned by the attention mechanism in Transformer models with different translation quality. We assess the representations of the encoder by extracting dependency relations based on self-attention weights, we perform four probing tasks to study the amount of syntactic and semantic captured information and we also test attention in a transfer learning scenario. Our analysis sheds light on the relative strengths and weaknesses of the various encoder representations. We observe that specific attention heads mark syntactic dependency relations and we can also confirm that lower layers tend to learn more about syntax while higher layers tend to encode more semantics.

papers.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine\n Translation
papers.research_question: How important are individual neurons for obtaining high-quality translations? Do individual neurons in NMT models contain interpretable linguistic information? Can we control MT output by intervening in the representation at the individual neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops unsupervised methods (based on correlations between models) for discovering important neurons in Neural Machine Translation models, shows these neurons impact translation quality and capture linguistic phenomena, and demonstrates how to control translations by modifying their activations.
papers.conclusion: The work indicates that not all information is distributed in NMT models, and that many human-interpretable grammatical and structural properties are captured by individual neurons. Moreover, modifying the activations of individual neurons allows controlling the translation output according to specified linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Unsupervised correlation methods (MaxCorr, MinCorr, LinReg, SVCCA) can rank neurons by importance, with top-ranked neurons having a larger impact on translation quality when erased.
Many top-ranked neurons capture interpretable linguistic properties such as position in sentence, parentheses, tense, number, gender, and noun phrase segmentation.
Modifying the activations of individual neurons (e.g., tense neurons) allows for controlling translation output (e.g., changing verb tense) with varying degrees of success.
Different ranking methods highlight different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find information distributed across tokens.
The work indicates that not all linguistic information in NMT models is fully distributed; some properties are captured by individual neurons.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional seq2seq).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Apply the methods to other tasks beyond machine translation.
papers.abstract:
Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing
substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such
information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to
individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important
neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models
learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision.
We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered
neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena.
Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by
modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: Probing for Arithmetic Errors in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can internal activations in language models be used to detect arithmetic errors?
papers.core_contribution: Simple probes can detect arithmetic errors from internal activations and enable lightweight self-correction via re-prompting.
papers.conclusion: Simple probes can extract predicted outputs and correct answers from internal activations, anticipate errors, generalize to chain-of-thought, and serve as weak oracles for self-correction.
papers.key_findings:
Probes can decode both the model's predicted output and the correct answer from hidden states with high accuracy.
Error detectors trained on these probes achieve over 90% accuracy in predicting model correctness.
Probes trained on simple arithmetic generalize to chain-of-thought reasoning on GSM8K problems.
Using error detectors to guide re-prompting corrects up to 11% of erroneous reasoning steps without degrading correct outputs.
Internal representations of numerical quantities are robust across contexts, enabling cross-setting generalization.
papers.limitation:
Focus on addition and subtraction, not other arithmetic operations like multiplication or division.
Experiments primarily on Gemma 2B IT, with limited evaluation on Phi-3.
Chain-of-thought analysis limited to addition-only GSM8K problems.
CoT evaluation uses structured equation formatting, not free-form natural language.
future_direction: Extend probing strategies to other arithmetic operations such as multiplication and division.
Broader evaluation across diverse architectures and model scales.
Explore other datasets with broader math coverage and varied reasoning formats.
Extend approach to operate over general, unstructured CoT traces.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether internal activations in language models can be used to detect arithmetic errors. Starting with a controlled setting of 3-digit addition, we show that simple probes can accurately decode both the model's predicted output and the correct answer from hidden states, regardless of whether the model's output is correct. Building on this, we train lightweight error detectors that predict model correctness with over 90% accuracy. We then extend our analysis to structured chain-of-thought traces on addition-only GSM8K problems and find that probes trained on simple arithmetic generalize well to this more complex setting, revealing consistent internal representations. Finally, we demonstrate that these probes can guide selective re-prompting of erroneous reasoning steps, improving task accuracy with minimal disruption to correct outputs. Our findings suggest that arithmetic errors can be anticipated from internal activations alone, and that simple probes offer a viable path toward lightweight model self-correction.

papers.title: From Next-Token to Mathematics: The Learning Dynamics of Mathematical Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does mathematical reasoning ability develop during pre-training and post-training in LLMs, and how aligned are the learning trajectories with human curricula?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MathCAMPS, a fine-grained dataset for mathematical reasoning, and uses it to analyze learning dynamics, showing that mathematical skills are learned in an order correlated with human curriculum and that instruction tuning has varied effects on different skills.
papers.conclusion: MathCAMPS enables fine-grained analysis of mathematical reasoning, revealing insights into learning dynamics and the effects of instruction tuning, paving the way for an empirical understanding of LLM training dynamics in relation to reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Mathematical skills are learned during pre-training in an order that measurably correlates with the human-designed curriculum, even though training data are randomly ordered.
Skills evolve smoothly during training rather than emerging discretely at specific points.
Instruction tuning has varied effects: it improves some mathematical skills but degrades others, and the impact depends on the specific tuning methodology.
Models struggle more with fraction operations than with decimal operations, likely due to tokenization differences and the multi-step reasoning required for fractions.
Models are not robust to follow-up questions, showing significant accuracy drops when probed with incremental or counterfactual questions.
papers.limitation: The evaluation only covers computational problems and does not capture conceptual mathematical skills that human students also learn.
future_direction: Using MathCAMPS to inform model pre-training and evaluation for educational applications.
Using follow-up problems in MathCAMPS as a rich source for further analysis of model robustness and dialogue understanding.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) solely trained on next-token prediction learn to solve a wide range of problems involving mathematical reasoning. But how does this ability evolve during training? We show the first analysis of how mathematical reasoning abilities of several open-weight LLMs develop during pre-training and post-training. To this end, we construct MathCAMPS, a synthetic dataset of novel mathematical reasoning problems grounded in 44 fine-grained skills taken from the Common Core curriculum from K to 8th grades. In one experiment, we show that mathematical skills are learned during pre-training in an order that measurably correlates with the human-designed curriculum, even though training data are randomly ordered. We also show a detailed analysis of which mathematical abilities benefit from instruction tuning, a widely used post-training method and, in contrast, which skills suffer. Our work paves the way for an empirical understanding of LLM training dynamics in relation to reasoning.

papers.title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning Dynamics and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the intrinsic dimensionality of layers in neural networks and how do learning dynamics evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SVCCA, a method for comparing neural network representations, and uses it to show that layers are over-parameterized, learning converges from bottom up, and proposes Freeze Training to save computation and improve generalization.
papers.conclusion: SVCCA is a powerful tool for comparing learned representations across layers, architectures, and time, providing insights into learning dynamics and motivating new training and compression techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimensionality of a layer is often much smaller than the number of neurons, indicating over-parameterization.
Learning dynamics show that networks converge from the bottom up, with lower layers solidifying before higher ones.
SVCCA can capture semantic similarities between classes, with similar classes having similar sensitivity patterns in the network.
Freeze Training, which sequentially freezes lower layers during training, can save computation and sometimes improve generalization.
The important directions found by SVCCA are distributed across many neurons rather than being axis-aligned.
papers.abstract: We propose a new technique, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA), a tool for quickly comparing two representations in a way that is both invariant to affine transform (allowing comparison between different layers and networks) and fast to compute (allowing more comparisons to be calculated than with previous methods). We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization; to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that simultaneously save computation and overfit less. Code: https://github.com/google/svcca/

papers.title: Multifaceted Feature Visualization: Uncovering the Different Types of Features Learned By Each Neuron in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we visualize the multiple different types of features (facets) that each neuron in a deep neural network responds to, given that neurons are multifaceted?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm that uncovers the multiple facets of each neuron and improves activation maximization image quality with more natural colors and coherent global structure.
papers.conclusion: The Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm improves the state of the art of activation maximization and provides a more comprehensive understanding of each neuron's function by revealing its multiple facets.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons in deep neural networks are multifaceted, responding to multiple types of features.
Higher-level neurons are more multifaceted than lower-level neurons.
The MFV algorithm produces visualizations with more natural colors and coherent global structure by separately synthesizing each facet.
The algorithm reveals that DNNs learn global structure, details, and context of objects, acting more like generative models.
A center-biased regularization technique reduces the repetition of object fragments in activation maximization images.
papers.limitation:
The number of unique images MFV produces for a unit depends on the manually set k in k-means; automatically identifying the true number of facets remains an open question.
It is unclear whether hidden fully connected layer neurons are truly amalgams of different concepts or part of distributed representations; current visualization methods (Deconv, LRP) do not conclusively reveal this.
future_direction: Future research is needed to understand the precise dynamics of why initializing with a mean facet image improves activation maximization quality.
Automatically identifying the true number of facets per neuron is an important open scientific question.
Further investigation into the function of hidden fully connected layer neurons and whether they are amalgams or represent abstract concepts.
papers.abstract: We can better understand deep neural networks by identifying which features each of their neurons have learned to detect. To do so, researchers have created Deep Visualization techniques including activation maximization, which synthetically generates inputs (e.g. images) that maximally activate each neuron. A limitation of current techniques is that they assume each neuron detects only one type of feature, but we know that neurons can be multifaceted, in that they fire in response to many different types of features: for example, a grocery store class neuron must activate either for rows of produce or for a storefront. Previous activation maximization techniques constructed images without regard for the multiple different facets of a neuron, creating inappropriate mixes of colors, parts of objects, scales, orientations, etc. Here, we introduce an algorithm that explicitly uncovers the multiple facets of each neuron by producing a synthetic visualization of each of the types of images that activate a neuron. We also introduce regularization methods that produce state-of-the-art results in terms of the interpretability of images obtained by activation maximization. By separately synthesizing each type of image a neuron fires in response to, the visualizations have more appropriate colors and coherent global structure. Multifaceted feature visualization thus provides a clearer and more comprehensive description of the role of each neuron.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
Figurative idioms receive more attention within the PIE in encoder self-attention compared to literal idioms.
Figurative idioms have reduced attention between the PIE and its context.
In cross-attention, figurative idioms lead to reduced attention on source-side PIE tokens and increased attention on the </s> token.
Hidden representations of figurative idioms change more across layers than those of literal idioms.
Intervening with INLP to remove linearly encoded features of figurativeness can change paraphrased translations to word-for-word, indicating a causal link.
papers.limitation:
Heuristic annotation method for translations has imperfect accuracy (75-89% for key categories).
Analysis is limited to seven European languages.
future_direction: Architectural changes to improve grouping of idioms as single units, e.g., training specific attention heads or penalizing overly compositional translations.
Evaluate the effect of compositionality-favouring techniques on non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.abstract: Unlike literal expressions, idioms' meanings do not directly follow from their parts, posing a challenge for neural machine translation (NMT). NMT models are often unable to translate idioms accurately and over-generate compositional, literal translations. In this work, we investigate whether the non-compositionality of idioms is reflected in the mechanics of the dominant NMT model, Transformer, by analysing the hidden states and attention patterns for models with English as source language and one of seven European languages as target language.When Transformer emits a non-literal translation - i.e. identifies the expression as idiomatic - the encoder processes idioms more strongly as single lexical units compared to literal expressions. This manifests in idioms' parts being grouped through attention and in reduced interaction between idioms and their context.In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens. These results suggest that Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions contributes to literal translations of idioms.

papers.title: Diverging views on the role of structured representations in linguistics and language modeling
papers.research_question: How do language models compare to human language processing in terms of structured representations, and what is their role in the science of language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that language models struggle with structured representations central to human language, and suggests that for language models to be effective models of language, structured representations must be incorporated as computational objects.
papers.conclusion: Language models need to conceptualize structured representations as computational objects to better align with human language and contribute to the science of language.
papers.key_findings:
Language models trained on next-word prediction may not learn structure-dependent representations necessary for human language.
Models like ChatGPT show insensitivity to Binding Principle C, incorrectly allowing co-reference in prohibited contexts.
Language models do not make a qualitative distinction between possible and impossible languages, treating them similarly unlike humans.
The internal representational infrastructure for possible and impossible languages overlaps in models, indicating no fundamental difference.
Incorporating structured representations as primary computational targets could enhance language models' utility as models of language.
future_direction: Incorporate structured representations as computational objects in language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recent years have seen dramatic advances in the linguistic abilities of language models, leading some authors to argue that they can be treated as models of language. Against this background, we provide a cognitive perspective on the place of language models in the science of language, with a particular focus on the role of structured representations. Evidence from linguistics, psychology and cognitive neuroscience shows that structured representations occupy a central place in the human mind. Structured representations constrain how linguistic forms map onto meanings, thereby determining the boundaries of possible human languages. In language modeling, instead, the place of structured representations is often peripheral. They are seen as optional end point of modeling, to be induced as a consequence of the objective the model tries to optimize – that is, next-word prediction. Because structured relations and representations are not necessarily useful for predicting the next word in a sequence, it is not guaranteed that the model’s internal organization will come to encode those representations. Indeed, contemporary language models struggle to use structured representations functionally to map form onto meaning, and to determine whether they should consider their input as a possible human language or not. Building on classic insights in linguistics and (computational) cognitive science, we suggest that any use of language models as models of language requires conceptualizing the role of structured representations as computational objects.

papers.title: Say Anything but This: When Tokenizer Betrays Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: How does tokenization, specifically non-unique token ID mappings, contribute to reasoning failures in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that a non-trivial fraction of reasoning failures in LLMs stems from the tokenizer's non-injective mapping between token ID sequences and surface strings, leading to 'phantom edits' where models change token IDs but output identical text.
papers.conclusion: Tokenizer-induced representational mismatches cause reasoning failures in LLMs, and scaling alone cannot resolve these deficiencies, motivating tokenizer-level remedies and more robust representational schemes.
papers.key_findings:
Tokenization non-uniqueness leads to 'phantom edits' where models output different token IDs for a target word while the decoded surface text remains identical.
A taxonomy of eight systematic tokenizer artifacts (e.g., whitespace-boundary shifts, intra-word resegmentation) is identified as the mechanisms behind these failures.
Model scaling does not eliminate these failures; they persist across model families and parameter sizes.
A token-ID masking intervention reduces phantom edits, indicating models possess the underlying reasoning capacity but are misled by tokenizer artifacts.
Most phantom edits (72.2%) preserve subtoken count (1→1 transitions) and are primarily due to whitespace-variant token pairs.
papers.limitation: The token-ID masking intervention is a post-hoc, superficial remedy that does not address the fundamental many-to-one mapping property of tokenization, and complete tokenizer redesign and model re-training remain computationally expensive.
future_direction: Test whether tokenization non-uniqueness affects reasoning behaviors beyond the replacement probe, such as chain-of-thought stability or multi-step arithmetic accuracy.
Develop tokenizer-aware training objectives that enforce representational consistency across equivalent encodings.
Redesign tokenizers to shrink equivalence classes, for example by eliminating duplicate forms of the same word.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reason over discrete token ID sequences, yet modern subword tokenizers routinely produce non-unique encodings: multiple token ID sequences can detokenize to identical surface strings. This representational mismatch creates an unmeasured fragility wherein reasoning processes can fail. LLMs may treat two internal representations as distinct "words" even when they are semantically identical at the text level. In this work, we show that tokenization can betray LLM reasoning through one-to-many token ID mappings. We introduce a tokenization-consistency probe that requires models to replace designated target words in context while leaving all other content unchanged. The task is intentionally simple at the surface level, enabling us to attribute failures to tokenizer-detokenizer artifacts rather than to knowledge gaps or parameter limitations. Through analysis of over 11000 replacement trials across state-of-the-art open-source LLMs, we find a non-trivial rate of outputs exhibit phantom edits: cases where models operate under the illusion of correct reasoning, a phenomenon arising from tokenizer-induced representational defects. We further analyze these cases and provide a taxonomy of eight systematic tokenizer artifacts, including whitespace-boundary shifts and intra-word resegmentation. These findings indicate that part of apparent reasoning deficiency originates in the tokenizer layer, motivating tokenizer-level remedies before incurring the cost of training ever-larger models on ever-larger corpora.

papers.title: Training Dynamics of Contextual N-Grams in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do contextual n-gram circuits form during training? Do they form gradually or in a sudden phase transition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that contextual n-gram circuits form gradually as second-order circuits, combining pre-existing n-gram and language detection circuits, contrary to the hypothesis that circuits form in sudden phase transitions.
papers.conclusion: The formation of the contextual n-gram circuit is gradual and represents a second-order circuit, adding complexity to the quantization model of neural scaling.
papers.key_findings:
The German context neuron and German trigram prediction are learned early in a phase transition, but the trigram prediction does not depend on the context neuron initially.
The contextual n-gram circuit (where trigram prediction depends on the context neuron) forms gradually later in training.
There is a large cohort of context neurons that form early but are quickly unlearned, and most have low impact on loss.
The direct effect of the context neuron boosts German unigrams, and the indirect effect enables contextual n-grams.
The general phase transition in capabilities coincides with the learning rate warm-up.
papers.limitation: The analysis focused on specifically selected n-grams that strongly rely on the German context neuron, and it is uncertain whether the neuron contributes to other circuits.
future_direction: Fully reverse-engineer the role of context neurons in language models by comprehensively identifying all circuits they are involved in or proving that unigram and n-gram effects are sufficient to explain their effects.
Investigate the emergence and role of the early context neurons that form and are quickly unlearned.
papers.abstract: Prior work has shown the existence of contextual neurons in language models, including a neuron that activates on German text. We show that this neuron exists within a broader contextual n-gram circuit: we find late layer neurons which recognize and continue n-grams common in German text, but which only activate if the German neuron is active. We investigate the formation of this circuit throughout training and find that it is an example of what we call a second-order circuit. In particular, both the constituent n-gram circuits and the German detection circuit which culminates in the German neuron form with independent functions early in training - the German detection circuit partially through modeling German unigram statistics, and the n-grams by boosting appropriate completions. Only after both circuits have already formed do they fit together into a second-order circuit. Contrary to the hypotheses presented in prior work, we find that the contextual n-gram circuit forms gradually rather than in a sudden phase transition. We further present a range of anomalous observations such as a simultaneous phase transition in many tasks coinciding with the learning rate warm-up, and evidence that many context neurons form simultaneously early in training but are later unlearned.

papers.title: Math Neurosurgery: Isolating Language Models' Math Reasoning Abilities Using Only Forward Passes
papers.research_question: How is math reasoning encoded in LLM parameters, and can math-specific parameters be isolated to improve math performance without affecting general language abilities?
papers.core_contribution: MathNeuro is a method to isolate math-specific parameters in LLMs using only forward passes; pruning these parameters deletes math ability without affecting general language, and scaling them improves math performance by 4-35%.
papers.conclusion: MathNeuro successfully isolates math-specific parameters, enabling targeted interventions to enhance math reasoning without compromising other abilities.
papers.key_findings:
MathNeuro isolates math-specific parameters by filtering out parameters important for general language tasks.
Pruning MathNeuro-identified parameters destroys math reasoning ability with minimal impact on non-math tasks.
Scaling these parameters improves math performance by 4-17% on GSM8K and 5-35% on MATH.
MathNeuro is data-efficient, effective even with a single sample.
Math-specific parameters are distributed throughout decoder blocks, not concentrated in specific layers.
future_direction: Applying MathNeuro to other skills or domains
Investigating the impact of different non-math datasets
Studying the theoretical underpinnings
papers.abstract: Math reasoning is an active area of Large Language Model (LLM) research because it is a hallmark of artificial intelligence and has implications in several domains, including math education. However, few works have explored how math reasoning is encoded within LLM parameters and if it is a skill that can be isolated within models. Doing so could allow targeted intervention to improve math performance without altering non-math behavior and foster understanding of how models encode math reasoning. We introduce Math Neurosurgery (MathNeuro), a computationally efficient method we use to isolate math-specific parameters in LLMs using only forward passes. MathNeuro builds on existing work by using weights and activations to calculate parameter importance, but isolates math-specific parameters by filtering out those important for general language tasks. Through pruning parameters MathNeuro identifies, we delete a LLM's math reasoning ability without significantly impacting its general language ability. Scaling the identified parameters by a small constant improves a pretrained or instruction-tuned LLM's performance by 4-17% on GSM8K and 5-35% on MATH while leaving non-math behavior unaltered. MathNeuro is also data efficient: most of its effectiveness holds when identifying math-specific parameters using a single sample. MathNeuro highlights the potential for future work to intervene on math-specific parameters.

papers.title: Does Circuit Analysis Interpretability Scale? Evidence from Multiple Choice Capabilities in Chinchilla
papers.research_question: Does circuit analysis interpretability scale to large language models, specifically for the algorithmic task of multiple-choice question answering?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that existing circuit analysis techniques (logit attribution, attention pattern visualization, activation patching) scale to a 70B parameter model, allowing identification and partial understanding of the circuit for multiple-choice question answering, particularly 'correct letter' heads.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analysis techniques can scale to large models, but the features used to implement algorithmic tasks can be messy in their semantics, even when limited to a distribution with little superposition.
papers.key_findings:
Identified 45 nodes (attention heads and MLPs) that are causally responsible for most of the model's performance on the multiple-choice task.
Categorized attention heads into four types: 'Correct Letter', 'Uniform', 'Single Letter', and 'Amplification'.
Found that 'correct letter' heads attend to the correct answer label and copy it to the output logits.
Used SVD to compress query/key/value subspaces of 'correct letter' heads, finding the query and key subspaces represent an 'Nth item in an enumeration' feature, but this is only a partial explanation for behavior on a more general distribution.
Showed that the algorithmic task of mapping the correct answer to its label is interpretable, but the specific features used are messy and only partially understood.
papers.limitation:
The effect of patching a node can be compensated by downstream nodes (backup behavior), potentially distorting results.
The analysis only finds a cross-section of the circuit (nodes separating ancestors and descendants) rather than the full set of relevant nodes.
Results are only applicable to the specific distribution tested (MMLU subset).
Focused on the net effect on the correct label, neglecting the part of the circuit that identifies the set of possible answer tokens.
future_direction: Investigating the rest of the circuit (nodes feeding into the correct letter heads).
Comparing different approaches to causal interventions (e.g., noising vs. denoising).
Automating circuit analysis to reduce labor intensity.
papers.abstract: \emph{Circuit analysis} is a promising technique for understanding the internal mechanisms of language models. However, existing analyses are done in small models far from the state of the art. To address this, we present a case study of circuit analysis in the 70B Chinchilla model, aiming to test the scalability of circuit analysis. In particular, we study multiple-choice question answering, and investigate Chinchilla's capability to identify the correct answer \emph{label} given knowledge of the correct answer \emph{text}. We find that the existing techniques of logit attribution, attention pattern visualization, and activation patching naturally scale to Chinchilla, allowing us to identify and categorize a small set of `output nodes' (attention heads and MLPs). We further study the `correct letter' category of attention heads aiming to understand the semantics of their features, with mixed results. For normal multiple-choice question answers, we significantly compress the query, key and value subspaces of the head without loss of performance when operating on the answer labels for multiple-choice questions, and we show that the query and key subspaces represent an `Nth item in an enumeration' feature to at least some extent. However, when we attempt to use this explanation to understand the heads' behaviour on a more general distribution including randomized answer labels, we find that it is only a partial explanation, suggesting there is more to learn about the operation of `correct letter' heads on multiple choice question answering.

papers.title: Superscopes: Amplifying Internal Feature Representations for Language Model Interpretation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret internal representations (like MLP outputs and hidden states) in language models that are not interpretable with existing self-interpretation methods, by amplifying weak features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Superscopes, a method that amplifies weak features in internal representations (MLP outputs and hidden states) to enable their interpretation via self-interpretation methods like Patchscopes, without requiring additional training.
papers.conclusion: Superscopes extends Patchscopes by amplifying internal representations, enabling interpretation of previously uninterpretable MLP outputs and hidden states, and draws a parallel to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models.
papers.key_findings:
Amplifying MLP outputs reveals meaningful interpretations that are not accessible with standard Patchscopes.
Amplifying hidden states can reveal interpretations in layers before contextualization occurs.
The amplification technique is analogous to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models, as both amplify directional shifts.
The Superscopes framework can automatically identify optimal amplification factors for interpretation.
The method demonstrates that weak features in internal representations can be amplified to reveal semantic content.
papers.limitation:
The method does not currently handle attention outputs, which may have a denser superposition of features.
The method for selecting the optimal amplifier may not be fully effective and could be improved.
future_direction: Extracting meaning from attention outputs.
Developing more effective approaches for selecting the optimal amplifier.
Exploring alternative ways to amplify meaning within Superscopes, such as using a different base vector for patching.
papers.abstract: Understanding and interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains an open challenge. Patchscopes introduced a method for probing internal activations by patching them into new prompts, prompting models to self-explain their hidden representations. We introduce Superscopes, a technique that systematically amplifies superposed features in MLP outputs (multilayer perceptron) and hidden states before patching them into new contexts. Inspired by the "features as directions" perspective and the Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) approach from diffusion models, Superscopes amplifies weak but meaningful features, enabling the interpretation of internal representations that previous methods failed to explain-all without requiring additional training. This approach provides new insights into how LLMs build context and represent complex concepts, further advancing mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: How Do Vision Transformers Work?
papers.research_question: How do multi-head self-attentions (MSAs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) work? Specifically, what properties of MSAs improve optimization, how do MSAs differ from convolutional layers (Convs), and how can we harmonize MSAs with Convs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that MSAs in Vision Transformers act as generalized spatial smoothing, flattening loss landscapes and improving generalization, and are complementary to convolutional layers as low-pass vs. high-pass filters. Based on these insights, the paper proposes AlterNet, a model that alternates Conv and MSA blocks, which outperforms CNNs even on small datasets.
papers.conclusion: MSAs are generalized spatial smoothings that complement Convs, and harmonizing them via an alternating pattern leads to models that outperform CNNs across data regimes.
papers.key_findings:
MSAs improve accuracy and generalization by flattening loss landscapes, primarily due to data specificity rather than long-range dependency.
MSAs are low-pass filters that reduce high-frequency signals and aggregate feature maps, while Convs are high-pass filters that amplify high-frequency signals and diversify feature maps.
ViTs suffer from non-convex losses in small data regimes, which can be alleviated by large datasets or loss landscape smoothing methods.
Multi-stage neural networks behave like series connections of small individual models, and MSAs at the end of a stage play a key role in prediction.
The proposed AlterNet, which alternates Conv and MSA blocks, outperforms CNNs not only on large datasets but also on small datasets.
papers.limitation: The effects of data augmentation on loss landscapes and uncertainty calibration require further investigation.
future_direction: Further investigation into the effects of data augmentation on uncertainty calibration and loss landscapes.
papers.abstract: The success of multi-head self-attentions (MSAs) for computer vision is now indisputable. However, little is known about how MSAs work. We present fundamental explanations to help better understand the nature of MSAs. In particular, we demonstrate the following properties of MSAs and Vision Transformers (ViTs): (1) MSAs improve not only accuracy but also generalization by flattening the loss landscapes.
